Now, the president favors giving Americans the option of joining a government-run plan that would compete with private insurers.  Watch more on the health care debate » . "Nobody is talking about some government takeover of health care. I'm tired of hearing that," Obama said in Raleigh, North Carolina, on Thursday. But Scheiner says that nobody has seen the details of that option, making it a hard sell for the president. "We don't even fully know what the public option is going to be. If the public option is too good, patients who are sick will flock to it, and I'm not sure it will be able to support itself." Scheiner almost had a chance to confront the president with his concerns. He was invited to a recent televised town hall meeting with Obama, but he says he was dropped from the program. outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — President Obama often speaks about the many forces aligned against his health care plan. But one critic has remained relatively quiet in the debate: Dr. David Scheiner, who served as Obama’s personal physician for 22 years.

Scheiner, a Chicago, Illinois-based doctor, has taken a hard look at the president’s prescription for health care reform—and he sees bad medicine.

“This isn’t the kind of health care program that I think is going to work,” he said.

What makes Scheiner’s criticism particularly noteworthy? In addition to serving as Obama’s personal physician for 22 years, he voted for the former Illinois senator in the 2008 presidential election.

Scheiner believes the president’s plan does not go far enough. In his view, the proposal’s greatest flaw is that “private insurers continue to be a part of the health scheme.”

Watch Scheiner discuss his objections »

“Everybody keeps saying we don’t want the government involved in health care,” Scheiner said in an interview. “But the government is involved in Medicare, and it works.”

Scheiner would prefer that the nation adopt a single-payer system similar to those in Canada and Europe. Such a financing system relies on one “payer”—which could be a government-run agency—to cover all health care costs billed by doctors, hospitals and other health professionals.

Advocates say the benefit is that costly administrative expenses are reduced, resulting in substantial savings for patients.

It is an approach that an up-and-coming state Sen. Obama discussed six years ago.

“I happen to be a proponent of a single-payer universal health care plan. ... But as all of you know, we may not get there immediately, because first we’ve got to take back the White House, and we’ve got to take back the Senate, and we’ve got to take back the House,” Obama said in 2003.

That position evolved during the presidential campaign.

“If I were designing a system from scratch, then I’d probably set up a single-payer system. But the problem is we’re not starting from scratch,” Obama said in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in August 2008.

The president now favors giving Americans the option of joining a government-run plan that would compete with private insurers.

Watch more on the health care debate »

“Nobody is talking about some government takeover of health care. I’m tired of hearing that,” Obama said Thursday in Raleigh, North Carolina.

Scheiner, however, says no one has seen the details of that option, making it a difficult proposal for the president to sell.

“We don’t even fully know what the public option is going to be. If the public option is too good, patients who are sick will flock to it, and I’m not sure it will be able to support itself.”

Scheiner nearly had an opportunity to confront the president with his concerns. He was invited to a recent televised town hall meeting with Obama, but he says he was dropped from the program.

“I just hope that the Congress, the American public and the president will hear some of my words,” he said. “We’ve got to do something better.”

Scheiner finally had an opportunity to make his case Thursday. He and other doctors who support a single-payer system gathered in Washington to meet with lawmakers and rally supporters.

He may no longer be the president’s doctor, but Scheiner says he is trying to save the patient before it is too late.

CNN’s Ed Hornick and Brittany Cummings contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — President Obama frequently points to the many groups opposing his health care proposal, but one notable detractor had largely stayed out of the public discussion: Dr. David Scheiner, who served as Obama’s personal doctor for 22 years.

Scheiner, a physician based in Chicago, Illinois, has closely examined Obama’s approach to health care reform and believes it is unlikely to succeed. Despite treating Obama for more than two decades and voting for the former Illinois senator in the 2008 presidential election, Scheiner argues that the plan is not ambitious enough.

His chief objection is that private insurance companies would remain part of the nation’s health care system.

In an interview, Scheiner said people repeatedly object to government participation in health care, even though the government already administers Medicare successfully. He prefers a single-payer model similar to systems used in Canada and Europe.

Under such an arrangement, a single entity—potentially a government agency—would pay health care bills submitted by physicians, hospitals and other medical providers. Supporters contend that eliminating costly administrative overhead would produce substantial savings for patients.

Obama himself discussed that idea six years earlier, when he was an emerging Illinois state senator. In 2003, he said he supported universal health care through a single-payer system, while acknowledging that it could not be achieved immediately. He argued that supporters would first need to regain control of the White House, the Senate and the House of Representatives.

His position shifted during the presidential campaign. Speaking in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in August 2008, Obama said he would probably choose a single-payer structure if he were building the country’s health care system from the beginning. However, he noted that the United States already had an established system and was not starting over.

As president, Obama instead backed allowing Americans to enroll in a government-operated insurance plan that would compete with private insurers.

At an event in Raleigh, North Carolina, on Thursday, Obama rejected claims that his proposal amounted to a government takeover of health care and expressed frustration with that characterization.

Scheiner, however, said the public had not yet been shown enough information about the proposed government option, making it difficult for Obama to win support. He also warned that if the public plan offered especially strong coverage, sick patients might move to it in large numbers, potentially threatening its financial viability.

Scheiner nearly had an opportunity to raise these concerns directly with Obama. He had been invited to participate in a recent televised town hall meeting featuring the president, but said he was later removed from the program.

He said he hoped Congress, the American people and Obama would still listen to his views because, in his opinion, the country needed to pursue a better solution.

Scheiner was finally able to present his position on Thursday, when he joined other physicians who favor single-payer health care in Washington. The group met with legislators and rallied supporters.

Although Scheiner no longer serves as Obama’s doctor, he said he was now trying to rescue the health care “patient” before time ran out.

CNN’s Ed Hornick and Brittany Cummings contributed to the report.

Dr. David Scheiner, who served as Barack Obama’s personal physician for 22 years and supported him during the 2008 presidential election, publicly criticized Obama’s proposed health care reforms. Although Scheiner welcomed efforts to expand access to medical care, he argued that the plan did not go far enough. His main objection was that it preserved a central role for private insurance companies, which he viewed as a major source of excessive costs and administrative complexity.

Scheiner instead advocated a government-backed, single-payer health care system similar to models used in Canada and parts of Europe. Under such a system, the government would finance essential medical services, reducing reliance on private insurers. He pointed to Medicare as evidence that substantial government involvement in health care can work effectively in the United States.

Supporters of single-payer health care argue that it could simplify billing, reduce administrative overhead, and eliminate many costs associated with the private insurance industry. They contend that these efficiencies could produce significant savings for both patients and the broader health care system while ensuring more universal access to care.

Obama himself had expressed support for single-payer universal health care in 2003. During his presidential campaign, however, he adopted a more pragmatic approach. He argued that because the existing employer-based and private insurance system was already deeply established, replacing it entirely would be politically and practically difficult. His reform proposal therefore sought to expand coverage and regulate insurers while retaining much of the existing system.

Dr. David Scheiner, who served for years as Barack Obama’s personal physician, has criticized the administration’s approach to health care reform as too limited. Although the proposal seeks to expand insurance coverage and introduce new regulations, Scheiner argues that it leaves the existing private-insurance system largely intact. In his view, relying on private companies preserves many of the inefficiencies and gaps that have long made American health care costly and difficult to navigate.

Scheiner favors a government-run single-payer system in which one public program would finance essential medical care for the entire population. He contends that such a system could substantially reduce the administrative expenses associated with multiple insurers, complex billing practices, marketing, and disputes over coverage. The resulting savings, he argues, could be directed toward patient care rather than insurance-company overhead.

While acknowledging that the administration’s plan represents an effort to broaden access to health insurance, Scheiner believes it falls short of genuine universal coverage. Continuing to depend on private insurers, he says, risks leaving some people underinsured or burdened by premiums, deductibles, and other out-of-pocket costs. A single-payer model, by contrast, could offer more consistent benefits and ensure that access to care does not depend on employment, income, or the terms of a private policy.

Scheiner therefore concludes that the proposed reforms do not go far enough. Rather than modifying the existing insurance-based structure, he advocates replacing it with a simpler public financing system designed to cover everyone. In his assessment, single-payer health care would be more efficient, less administratively wasteful, and better able to deliver effective universal coverage.

## Obama’s former doctor criticizes health reform plan over lack of single-payer option

**WASHINGTON** — Dr. David Scheiner, who served as Barack Obama’s personal physician for more than two decades before Obama became president, criticized the administration’s health care reform effort, arguing that it failed to address the nation’s problems because it did not establish a single-payer system.

Scheiner said expanding the government’s role through a Medicare-for-all-style program would provide broader coverage while reducing administrative costs. He warned that reforms built around private insurance companies would leave the existing system largely intact.

The Chicago physician treated Obama for 22 years and had publicly supported his presidential campaign. But Scheiner said his familiarity with Obama did not prevent him from challenging the president’s approach to health policy.

His criticism underscored divisions among Democrats and health care advocates during the reform debate. While some progressives pushed for single-payer coverage, the Obama administration focused on proposals that would preserve employer-based and private insurance while expanding access, regulating insurers and offering subsidies to people who could not afford coverage.

Obama had previously expressed support for single-payer health care as a long-term goal but said that, as president, he had to work within the system already in place. Administration officials also argued that replacing private insurance outright lacked sufficient political support in Congress.

Scheiner maintained that anything short of a publicly financed universal system would fail to control costs and guarantee care for all Americans.

The debate ultimately led to the Affordable Care Act, signed by Obama in March 2010. The law expanded Medicaid, created insurance marketplaces and prohibited insurers from denying coverage because of pre-existing conditions, but it did not create a single-payer system.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on why David Scheiner, Obama’s doctor for 22 years and a 2008 supporter, opposes the president’s proposed public-option approach and wants private insurers removed from health care.
counterfactuals.output:
David Scheiner, Barack Obama’s Chicago physician for roughly 22 years and a supporter in the 2008 election, opposed Obama’s 2009 public-option strategy from the left—not because he objected to public insurance, but because he believed the proposed option was far too limited.

Scheiner favored a single-payer, “Medicare for All” system in which medical care would still be delivered largely by private doctors and hospitals, but financing would be handled by one public insurer. His objections included:

- **Private insurers would remain central to the system.** A public plan merely competing with them would preserve what he saw as the fundamental problems: profits, high executive pay, marketing costs, complicated billing, coverage denials, and interference in treatment.
- **Insurers could select healthier customers.** Scheiner warned that private companies would try to retain profitable, relatively healthy people while sicker and more expensive patients gravitated toward the public plan. That could make the public option appear costly or ineffective and politically undermine it.
- **It would not eliminate administrative waste.** Doctors and hospitals would still have to deal with numerous plans, rules, forms, networks, and reimbursement systems. Scheiner believed a single payer could redirect much of that spending toward actual care.
- **Universal coverage was not guaranteed.** In his view, subsidies, mandates, and a public option would leave gaps and retain financial barriers, whereas an expanded Medicare-type program could cover everyone automatically.
- **Obama had compromised too much with the health-care industry.** Scheiner was disappointed that the administration treated single payer as politically unrealistic and worked within a framework acceptable to insurers and other industry interests. He said Obama needed greater political courage and criticized the limited role given to single-payer advocates in the debate.

Thus, Scheiner’s position was not that government should stay out of health care. It was that a small public competitor inside an insurance-dominated market would be unstable and insufficient. He wanted private health insurers removed from the financing of basic care and replaced by a universal public insurance system.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a 2009 political news story examining Barack Obama’s shift from supporting single-payer health care in 2003 to advocating a government-run plan that competes with private insurers.
counterfactuals.output:
**Obama’s Health-Care Evolution: From Single Payer to a Public Option**  
*By Staff Writer | Washington, 2009*

WASHINGTON — Six years ago, Barack Obama told an Illinois labor audience that he supported a single-payer health-care system, in which the government would finance coverage for all Americans.

“I happen to be a proponent of a single-payer universal health care program,” Obama said in 2003, while serving in the Illinois Senate. But he also warned that the country could not move to such a system immediately, saying the first step was to elect Democrats and regain control of the White House and Congress.

Now, as president, Obama is pursuing a more limited—and more politically feasible—approach. Rather than replacing private insurance, he is calling for a government-run health plan that would compete with private insurers in a new marketplace for individuals and small businesses.

The shift has become a central point of contention in the health-care debate. Conservatives cite Obama’s earlier remarks as evidence that the proposed public plan could be a step toward government control of medicine. Liberal activists, meanwhile, accuse the president of retreating from an idea they believe would provide universal coverage more efficiently.

The White House says Obama’s position reflects practical judgment, not abandonment of his broader goals.

During the 2008 presidential campaign, Obama repeatedly said that if the United States were designing a health-care system from the beginning, a single-payer model might make sense. But with most insured Americans receiving coverage through employers, he argued that reform should build on existing arrangements rather than dismantle them.

Under the proposals being debated in Congress, people generally could keep employer-sponsored or private coverage. A public insurance option would be offered alongside private plans, with the administration arguing that government competition could lower premiums and force insurers to operate more efficiently.

That is substantially different from a single-payer system. Under single payer, the government typically finances medical coverage for the entire population, although doctors and hospitals may remain privately operated. A public option would instead be one insurer among several in a market that remained largely private.

Republicans and insurance-industry groups remain skeptical of that distinction. They argue that a government plan could receive advantages unavailable to private companies, allowing it to charge lower premiums and gradually drive competitors from the market.

“If the government sets the rules, regulates the market and also fields its own team, private insurers will not be competing on a level playing field,” opponents contend.

Administration officials say the public plan should operate under rules similar to those governing private insurers and deny that it is intended to eliminate private coverage. Obama has also resisted demands from some Democratic activists to make single payer the centerpiece of the legislation, emphasizing instead the need to expand coverage, prohibit insurance abuses and control rising costs.

The political calculation is clear. Single-payer legislation would face intense opposition not only from Republicans and the insurance industry, but also from moderate Democrats and many Americans satisfied with their current coverage. Even the public option has divided Democrats, particularly in the Senate, where rural-state and centrist members have questioned its cost and potential effect on private markets.

Obama’s evolution also illustrates the difference between expressing a long-term preference and governing within existing political and economic constraints. In 2003, he described single payer as a goal requiring a lengthy transition. In 2009, with an opportunity to enact the most significant health-care changes in decades, he is concentrating on a mixed system that preserves private insurance while adding a public competitor.

Whether that compromise can hold together Obama’s coalition remains uncertain. Progressive Democrats say a strong public option is the minimum necessary to challenge the insurance industry. Moderates are considering alternatives, including nonprofit cooperatives or a public plan that would become available only if private insurers fail to meet certain standards.

For Obama, the debate poses risks on both sides. If he presses too hard for a government plan, he could lose moderate lawmakers whose votes are essential. If he accepts legislation without one, he could alienate supporters who believed his election would produce a fundamental restructuring of American health care.

The president is no longer proposing the single-payer system he once endorsed. But by insisting that government should compete directly with private insurers, he is still asking Congress to grant Washington a larger role in providing health coverage—a change that supporters call necessary reform and opponents see as the opening move in a much broader transformation.

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Dr. David Scheiner, President Barack Obama’s longtime physician, said the administration’s health care proposals did not go far enough and argued that a single-payer system would provide broader, more efficient coverage.

Scheiner, who treated Obama for more than two decades in Chicago, said Medicare offered a model for universal coverage, despite its shortcomings.

“Medicare is a single-payer system,” Scheiner said. “It’s not perfect, but it works. People understand it, and it has far less administrative overhead than private insurance.”

He said he favored expanding Medicare to cover all Americans rather than preserving a system dominated by private insurers.

“I would like to see Medicare for everybody,” Scheiner said. “A single-payer plan is the only way to cover everyone and control costs.”

Obama has said that if the United States were creating a health care system from scratch, a single-payer approach could make sense. But the president has argued that replacing the existing employer-based system would be too disruptive.

Scheiner also expressed concern that the administration had not clearly defined the proposed government-run insurance plan intended to compete with private insurers.

“The public option is unclear,” he said. “Nobody seems to know exactly what it will be, who will be eligible or whether it will have enough strength to compete with the insurance companies.”

Scheiner said he had hoped to raise those concerns during a televised town hall on health care featuring Obama. He said he was initially contacted about participating but ultimately was not included in the broadcast.

“I was invited, and then I was disinvited,” Scheiner said. “I suppose they didn’t want someone there who would challenge the plan from the single-payer point of view.”

The White House did not immediately respond to Scheiner’s criticism. The television network hosting the event said decisions about participants were made by its producers, not the administration.

Scheiner emphasized that his disagreement was about policy rather than his former patient.

“I support the president,” he said. “But I don’t think this plan goes far enough. We need a system that covers everybody.”

# Obama’s Former Doctor Sees “Bad Medicine” in Health Care Prescription

**WASHINGTON —** Dr. David Scheiner spent more than two decades caring for Barack Obama before his former patient entered the White House. But when it came to the president’s health care agenda, the Chicago physician offered a blunt diagnosis: the proposed treatment did not go far enough.

Scheiner traveled to Washington in 2009 with other advocates of a single-payer health system to lobby members of Congress. Their prescription was a government-run program covering all Americans—an approach often described as “Medicare for All”—rather than the mix of private insurance, new regulations and subsidies being debated by lawmakers.

Scheiner argued that leaving private insurers at the center of the system would preserve high administrative costs and fail to guarantee universal coverage. Even a government-run insurance option, he said, would be inadequate if it merely competed alongside private plans.

“I don’t think he really understands,” Scheiner said of Obama’s approach at the time, criticizing what he viewed as an overly cautious compromise. Although he remained personally fond of his former patient, Scheiner said the administration’s health care prescription amounted to “bad medicine” because it treated the system’s symptoms without addressing its underlying structure.

His visit put an unusually personal face on a broader dispute within the Democratic coalition. Obama had expressed support for single-payer health care earlier in his political career, while also acknowledging that moving to such a system would be difficult because millions of Americans already received coverage through employers. As president, he pursued legislation designed to expand access while preserving much of the existing insurance market.

Single-payer supporters feared their preferred model was being pushed aside before the congressional debate had fully begun. Scheiner and fellow activists met with lawmakers and staff members, urging them to consider a national plan that would replace most private insurance with publicly financed coverage.

Their effort faced steep political obstacles. Democratic leaders were struggling to unite moderates and liberals around a bill, while Republicans broadly opposed the emerging proposals. Hospitals, drug companies, insurers and other industry groups also held significant influence over the negotiations.

Scheiner’s criticism stood out because of his long relationship with Obama. He had treated Obama at a Chicago medical practice beginning in the late 1980s, years before the future president became a national political figure. Yet Scheiner emphasized that his objections were professional and policy-based, not personal.

For the physician and his fellow advocates, the lobbying trip was about keeping single-payer reform visible during a debate increasingly focused on narrower alternatives. They contended that universal public coverage would give patients greater security, simplify billing and allow the government to negotiate lower costs.

The administration and its allies countered that a sweeping replacement of the existing system lacked enough support to pass Congress. They argued that expanding Medicaid, providing subsidies, regulating insurers and creating marketplaces represented the most politically achievable path toward broader coverage.

Congress ultimately passed the Affordable Care Act in 2010 without a single-payer program or a public insurance option. The law expanded coverage and imposed new rules on insurers but retained the central role of private insurance—precisely the outcome Scheiner had warned would fall short.

His Washington trip captured a tension that would continue long after the legislation became law: whether health care reform should build on the existing system or replace it with universal government insurance. For Obama’s former doctor, the answer was clear. Incremental reform was not enough; the country needed a different prescription.
